hypotheses.name: Positioning
hypotheses.reasoning: The premium repositioning is consistent across menu, stores and pricing, and almost no comment disputes it. People argue about how the name reads, not about where the brand is going.

hypotheses.name: Target Audience
hypotheses.reasoning: There is a visible split: design press praises the mark while app-ordering regulars complain. The only audience data is a small self-selected Reddit poll, so we cannot confirm the split is the cause rather than a symptom.

hypotheses.name: Differentiation
hypotheses.reasoning: A handful of comments call it generic, but most discussion says the opposite — the ligature is distinctive. Side-by-side comparisons with Harbor show the marks are easy to tell apart.

hypotheses.name: Message
hypotheses.reasoning: The launch promised a mark 'made for mobile ordering' and 'faster to recognise on small screens'. That claim is contradicted exactly where customers look, which turned a routine logo complaint into a widely shared joke.

hypotheses.name: Creative Execution
hypotheses.reasoning: The 'rt' ligature shares a stem and aligns the t's crossbar with the r's arm, so below roughly 60px the t vanishes and the mark reads 'Norhwind'. An informal 20-person test reproduces it at icon size but not at poster size.

hypotheses.name: Competition
hypotheses.reasoning: Harbor's same-day fall campaign drew no cross-mentions and share of voice shows no spike. Commenters themselves describe it as a typography story, not a competitor story.

diagnosis.main_cause: At app-icon and cup-sleeve sizes, the new 'rt' ligature collapses into a single stroke, so the wordmark reads as 'Norhwind' — a different word.
diagnosis.explanation: Most negative reactions cite legibility, not taste: customers screenshot the loyalty-app icon and cup stamp, where the t disappears into the r (ev_003, ev_013, ev_032). A 20-person informal test reproduces the misreading at icon size but not at poster size (ev_021). The identity was only reviewed and published at billboard and storefront scale (ev_017). Because the launch promised a mark 'made for mobile ordering', the failure landed on the brand's own claim and spread as a meme (ev_005, ev_015).
secondary_causes: The launch message promised small-screen legibility, so the defect read as a broken promise rather than an aesthetic choice.
No small-size cut of the wordmark was shipped for the app icon and cup stamp, unlike comparable app-first rebrands.
A recent price increase made some customers less forgiving of the change.
diagnosis.surprising_finding: This is not a repeat of 2014. That backlash was about losing a 'cosy feel' and faded in six weeks; this one is about the name being misread, and it comes mostly from app-ordering regulars — the exact audience the redesign was meant for — while the design press, who saw it only at poster size, praised it.

prescription.change: Open the 'rt' ligature: separate the stems and drop the t's crossbar below the r's arm.
prescription.why: The misreading comes from the shared stem; separating it keeps the condensed style that reviewers liked.

prescription.change: Ship a dedicated small-size cut (wider tracking, heavier t) for the app icon, favicon and cup stamp.
prescription.why: Every complaint cluster is at 48–64px or on the 3 cm stamp; comparable app-first rebrands use an optical size or monogram there.

prescription.change: Relaunch with a short legibility-first film that shows the fixed mark at icon size first, billboard last.
prescription.why: The original launch was judged at billboard scale; reversing the order addresses the broken 'made for mobile' promise directly.

prescription.change: Acknowledge the 'Norhwind' joke in one owned post instead of 'it will grow on people'.
prescription.why: The 2014 framing doesn't fit: this is a fixable defect, and the brand response currently reads as dismissive.

creative_brief.concept: "Every letter, every size." The refined wordmark is introduced where it failed — on a phone home screen and a cup sleeve — before it scales up to the storefront.
creative_brief.message: We heard you: Northwind now reads as Northwind, from the app icon to the sign above the door.
creative_brief.audience: App-ordering regulars who saw 'Norhwind' on their phone and cup; secondarily, the design community following the story.
creative_brief.tone: Warm, self-aware, a little playful — owning the mistake without grovelling.
scenes: Close-up of a phone home screen at morning light; the new Northwind icon is crisp and unmistakable.
A barista's hand slides a cup across the counter; the stamp on the sleeve is clearly legible.
Slow pull-back from the cup to the storefront sign, the same wordmark at large scale.
End card: the refined wordmark alone on cream, with the line 'Every letter, every size.'
creative_brief.visual_direction: Natural morning light, warm cream and espresso-brown palette, shallow depth of field, calm handheld camera. No visual effects, no on-screen text except the end card.
creative_brief.cta: Update the app — and see your Northwind.

before_after.after: Separated r and t, wider small-size tracking
Dedicated cut for app icon, favicon and cup stamp

before_after.before: "Made for mobile ordering" — contradicted by the icon
before_after.after: "Every letter, every size" — shown at icon size first
Phone and cup first, billboard last
Owns the 'Norhwind' joke and shows the fix

generic_check.note: The diagnosis names a specific glyph pair ('rt'), a size threshold (~60px) and the touchpoints where it fails (app icon, cup stamp). It would not fit another brand's campaign unchanged.
